source_text: Paulus vero Apostolus de persecutore, qui primus Ecclesiae sanguinem fudit, postea gladium stylo mutans, et convertens machaeram in aratrum; lupus rapax Benjamin, dehinc ipse afferens escam secundum Jacob, qualiter martyria, jam et sibi optabilia, commendat! cum de Thessalonicensibus gaudens: Uti, inquit, gloriemur in vobis in Ecclesiis Dei pro tolerantia vestra et fide, in omnibus persecutionibus et pressuris, quibus sustinetis ostentamen justi judicii Dei, ut digni habeamini regno ejus, pro quo et patimini. Sicut et ad Romanos: Non solum autem, verum etiam exultantes in pressuris; certi quod pressura tolerantiam perficit, tolerantia vero probationem, probatio autem spem, spes vero non confundit. Et rursus: Quod si filii, et haeredes; haeredes quidem Dei, cohaeredes vero Christi: siquidem compatimur, uti et cum illo glorificemur. Reputo enim passiones hujus temporis non esse dignas ad gloriam, quae in nobis revelabitur. Et ideo postmodum: Quis, inquit, separabit nos a dilectione Christi? pressura, an angustia, an fames, an nuditas, an periculum, an machaera, secundum quod scriptum est: tui caussa mortificamur tota die, deputati sumus ut pecora jugulationis; sed in omnibus istis supervincimus pro eo qui nos dilexit. Persuasum enim habemus, quod neque mors, neque vita, neque virtus, neque sublimitas, neque profundum, neque alia conditio poterit nos a dilectione Dei separare, quae est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Sed et Corinthiis passiones suas enumerans, patiendum utique praefinivit: In laboribus abundantius, in carceribus plurimum, in mortibus saepius; a Judaeis quinquies quadragenas citra unam accepi, ter virgis caesus, semel lapidatus, et reliqua. Quae si magis incommoda quam martyria videbuntur, tamen rursus: Propter quod, inquit, boni duco in infirmitatibus, in injuriis, in necessitatibus, in persecutionibus, in angustiis pro Christo. Etiam in superioribus: Qui in omnibus tribulemur, sed non coangustemur; et indigeamus, sed non perindigeamus; quoniam persecutionibus agitemur, sed non derelinquamur; qui dejiciamur, sed non pereamus: semper mortificationem Christi Jesu in corpore nostro circumferentes. Sed etsi, inquit, exterior homo noster vitiatur, caro scilicet, vi persecutionum; sed interior renovatur die et die; anima scilicet spe promissionum. Nam quod ad praesens, temporale et leve pressurae nostrae per supergressum in supergressum aeternum pondus gloriae perficit nobis, non intuentibus quae videntur, sed quae non videntur. Quae enim videntur, temporalia, de incommodis dicens; quae vero non videntur, aeterna, de praemiis spondens. Thessalonicensibus vero de vinculis scribens, utique beatos affirmavit,, quibus donatum esset non tantum credere in Christum, sed etiam pro ipso pati: Eumdem, inquit, agonem habentes quem in me vidistis, et nunc audistis. Nam et si libor super sacrificium, gaudeo et congaudeo omnibus vobis, perinde et vos gaudete et congaudete mihi. Vides quam martyrii definiat felicitatem, cui de gaudio mutuo acquirit solemnitatem. Ut proximus denique voti sui factus est, qualiter de prospectu ejus exsultans Timotheo scribit? Ego enim jam libor, et tempus dijunctionis instat. Agonem bonum decertavi, cursum consummavi, fidem custodivi; superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet, scilicet passionis. Satis et ipse supra allocutus: Fidelis sermo: si enim commortui sumus Christo, et convivemus; si sufferimus, et conregnabimus; si negaverimus, et ille nos negabit; si non credimus, ille fidelis est, negare se non potest. Ne ergo confundaris martyrio Domini nostri, neque me vinctum ejus; quia praedixerat: Non enim dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sanae mentis. Virtute enim patimur ex dilectione in Deum, et sana mente, cum ob innocentiam patimur. Sed et sicubi tolerantiam praecipit, quibus magis eam quam passionibus prospicit? sicubi ab idololatria divellit, quid ei magis quam martyria praevellit?
pass_a_gloss: Paul, however, an Apostle, concerning a persecutor, who first shed the Church's blood, later changing the sword to a stylus and converting the sword to a plow; a rapacious wolf of Benjamin, thereafter himself bringing food according to Jacob, in what way he commends martyrdoms, now already desirable to him! When he is rejoicing about the Thessalonians: We glory, he says, in you in the Churches of God for your endurance and faith, in all the persecutions and pressures that you endure, a demonstration of God's just judgment, so that you may be considered worthy of His kingdom, for which you also suffer. Just as he also says to the Romans: Not only, however, but also rejoicing in pressures; certain that pressure perfects endurance, endurance truly proves testing, testing indeed hope, hope however does not disappoint. And again: If we are sons, then also heirs; heirs indeed of God, but co-heirs of Christ: if we suffer, so that we may also be glorified with Him. I consider the sufferings of this time not to be worthy of the glory that will be revealed in us. And therefore afterwards: Who, he says, will separate us from the love of Christ? Pressure, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or sword, according to what is written: We are killed all day for Your sake, we are considered as sheep for slaughter; but in all these things we overcome on account of Him who loved us. For we are convinced that neither death, nor life, nor virtue, nor height, nor depth, nor any other condition will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. But also to the Corinthians, enumerating his own sufferings, he certainly defined what must be suffered: In labors more abundantly, in prisons more frequently, in deaths often; from the Jews I received forty lashes minus one five times, I was beaten with rods three times, I was stoned once, and the rest. If these seem more like hardships than martyrdoms, nevertheless again: On account of which, he says, I consider it good to be in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ. Also in the preceding words: We are troubled in every way, but not constrained; we are in need, but not in extreme need; we are persecuted, but not abandoned; we are struck down, but not destroyed: always carrying the death of Christ Jesus in our body. But if, he says, our outer man is being destroyed, namely the flesh, by the power of persecutions; but our inner man is being renewed day by day; namely the soul, by the hope of promises. For what is present, our temporary and light pressure is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond measure, not looking at what is seen, but at what is not seen. For what is seen is temporary, speaking about hardships; what is not seen, however, is eternal, promising rewards. To the Thessalonians, however, writing about his chains, he certainly affirmed that those are blessed to whom it has been given not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for Him: Having, he says, the same struggle that you saw in me and now hear. For even if I am poured out as a sacrifice, I rejoice and congratulate all of you, and in the same way you also rejoice and congratulate me. You see how he defines the happiness of martyrdom, acquiring solemnity from mutual joy. So that, having become the next one to fulfill his vow, he writes to Timothy, exulting about his prospect? For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; there remains a crown, which the Lord will give me on that day, namely the crown of martyrdom. It is sufficient that he also spoke above: A faithful word: if we have died with Christ, and we live; if we suffer, we will also reign; if we deny, He will also deny us; if we do not believe, He is faithful, He cannot deny Himself. Therefore, do not be ashamed of the martyrdom of our Lord, nor of me being bound for Him; because He predicted: For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power and love and a sound mind. For we suffer with power from love for God, and with a sound mind, when we suffer for innocence. But also, wherever he commands endurance, to whom does he foresee it more than to those who suffer martyrdom? Wherever he tears away from idolatry, what does he tear away more than martyrdoms?

pass_b_english: Paul the apostle began as a persecutor who shed the church's blood first, then swapped his sword for a stylus and hammered his blade into a plow. He was Benjamin the ravenous wolf; afterward he brought food himself, just as Jacob said. That is how he commends martyrdoms, which have now become desirable even to him. He rejoices over the Thessalonians: we glory in you among God's churches because of your endurance and faith in all the persecutions and pressures you bear, a demonstration of God's just judgment, so that you may be counted worthy of his kingdom, for which you are also suffering (2 Thessalonians 1:4-5). He says the same to the Romans: not only that, but we also exult in our pressures, knowing that pressure produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, proven character produces hope, and hope does not disappoint (Romans 5:3-5). And again: if we are children, then we are heirs — heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ — provided we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17). I consider the sufferings of this present time not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us (Romans 8:18). Therefore he adds: who will separate us from the love of Christ? Pressure, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? As scripture says, 'For your sake we are killed all day long; we are accounted as sheep for slaughter.' Yet in all these things we prevail through the one who loved us. For I am convinced that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 8:35-39). To the Corinthians he itemizes his own sufferings, defining what must be endured: in labors more abundantly, in prisons more frequently, in deaths often; from the Jews five times I received forty lashes minus one, three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, and the rest (2 Corinthians 11:23-25). If these look more like hardships than martyrdoms, he says again: for Christ's sake I take pleasure in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in distresses (2 Corinthians 12:10). Earlier he wrote: we are afflicted in every way but not crushed; perplexed but not driven to despair; persecuted but not forsaken; struck down but not destroyed — always carrying in the body the death of Jesus (2 Corinthians 4:8-10). So if our outer self is wasting away — the flesh, by the force of persecutions — our inner self is being renewed day by day — the soul, by the hope of promises. For this slight momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison, because we look not at what is seen but at what is unseen; what is seen is transient, but what is unseen is eternal (2 Corinthians 4:16-18). Writing to the Thessalonians about his chains, he declares blessed those to whom it has been granted not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him, since they share the same conflict they saw in him and now hear about (Philippians 1:29-30). Even if I am poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice of your faith, I rejoice and share my joy with you all; you likewise should rejoice and share your joy with me (Philippians 2:17-18). You see how he defines the happiness of martyrdom, gaining solemnity from mutual joy. Having become the next to fulfill his vow, he writes to Timothy exulting in his prospect: I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day — the crown of martyrdom (2 Timothy 4:6-8). It suffices that he also said above: the saying is trustworthy — if we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he will also deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2:11-13). So do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner; for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control (2 Timothy 1:8, 7). We suffer with power, from love for God, and with a sound mind, because we suffer for innocence. And wherever he commands endurance, for whom does he foresee it more than for martyrs? Wherever he tears people from idolatry, what does he tear them toward more than martyrdom?

review.notes: Pass B adds significant content not present in the Locked Latin source, specifically expanding the quote from Romans 8:35-39 to include 'nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor anything else in all creation' which is not in the Latin text provided. It also adds 'the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me' in the Timothy section, whereas the Latin only says 'superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet, scilicet passionis'.
reasons: Pass B adds content not found in the Locked Latin: 'nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor anything else in all creation' (compared to 'neque mors, neque vita, neque virtus, neque sublimitas, neque profundum, neque alia conditio') and 'the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me' (compared to 'superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet, scilicet passionis').

review.notes: source: 'Paulus vero Apostolus de persecutore, qui primus Ecclesiae sanguinem fudit, postea gladium stylo mutans, et convertens machaeram in aratrum; lupus rapax Benjamin, dehinc ipse afferens escam secundum Jacob, qualiter martyria, jam et sibi optabilia, commendat! cum de Thessalonicensibus gaudens: Uti, inquit, gloriemur in vobis in Ecclesiis Dei pro tolerantia vestra et fide, in omnibus persecutionibus et pressuris, quibus sustinetis ostentamen justi judicii Dei, ut digni habeamini regno ejus, pro quo et patimini.' english: 'Paul the apostle began as a persecutor who shed the church's blood first, then swapped his sword for a stylus and hammered his blade into a plow. He was Benjamin the ravenous wolf; afterward he brought food himself, just as Jacob said. That is how he commends martyrdoms, which have now become desirable even to him.'
reasons: The translation fails to preserve the full sense of the Latin text, omitting key elements such as 'qualiter martyria, jam et sibi optabilia, commendat!' which means 'how he commends martyrdoms, now also desirable to him!' The omission of 'jam et sibi optabilia' (now also desirable to him) alters the meaning of the passage.
